title: Incident Response
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Incident Response.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Incident Response and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Incident Response, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 22: Security Logging, Monitoring, and Incident Response. It builds practical understanding of Incident Response with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Incident Response turns a security intention into evidence, an operational owner, and a repeatable control. Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.

content_blocks.title: Visual model: Incident Response
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-stage visual model for Incident Response: Capture security event; Redact sensitive values; Correlate signals; Respond + retest.
content_blocks.caption: Concept map for Incident Response. It is a learning aid, not a substitute for the stated control conditions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Incident Response can be understood through this sequence: Capture security event → Redact sensitive values → Correlate signals → Respond + retest. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 165.1 Incident identification and classification; 165.2 Containment and impact assessment; 165.3 Credential and token revocation; 165.4 Preserving evidence; 165.5 Recovery and secure restoration; 165.6 Lessons learned and corrective actions. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Incident Response
content_blocks.expected_output: A structured security event provides correlation and outcome context without storing a password, session token, or raw sensitive payload.
content_blocks.run_instructions: All values are synthetic. Avoid logging credentials, access tokens, payment data, or unnecessary personal information; apply retention and access controls to logs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Incident Response”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Incident Response in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Incident Response is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Record useful security events with correlation context but without secrets, define alert/escalation and response steps, preserve necessary evidence, and verify recovery or remediation.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
